stickers.title: The cookie standoff
lesson: Two creatures, one cookie. If both share, each gets half.
If one grabs and the other shares, the grabber gets the whole cookie.
So each one does better alone by grabbing. But when both grab, the cookie breaks and both lose. This trap is the prisoner's dilemma.

stickers.title: Copy that
lesson: Echo shares the first cookie. After that, Echo does what its partner did last time.
Against a grabber, Echo grabs back, and nobody eats.
When a game repeats, a kind player who copies back can do very well. But one mistake can start a feud that never ends.
stickers.tryThis: Give the berry bush to four strangers.

stickers.title: The last berry
lesson: Four strangers find one bush. Each takes just one more, and Gulp takes two.
Soon the bush is bare, and nobody gets berries tomorrow. This is the tragedy of the commons.
Friends who trust each other take turns, and the bush lives.
stickers.tryThis: Put three creatures by the signpost.

stickers.title: Look up
lesson: Three creatures stare where the sign points.
Others see them and join in. Nothing is there.
We copy a crowd to fit in, or because we think the crowd knows something. Sometimes the crowd copies nothing at all.
stickers.tryThis: Drop someone in the puddle while friends watch.

stickers.title: Somebody should
lesson: With one friend near, help comes at once.
With many near, each one waits for someone else to act.
This is the bystander effect. When you see a problem, act as if you are the only one who can help.
stickers.tryThis: Poke Bell, then walk Bell to the mirror.

stickers.title: Nobody noticed
stickers.riddle: A smudge, a mirror, and a panic.
lesson: Bell sees a smudge in the mirror and panics. Then Bell checks each friend.
Each friend is busy with their own thoughts.
We think others notice our flaws much more than they do. This is the spotlight effect.
stickers.tryThis: Drop someone into the left twin box.

stickers.title: Which one is me?
stickers.riddle: Two boxes, one friend, two friends.
lesson: Glim goes into the left box. Glim also comes out of the right box.
Both have the same body and the same memories. Both say they are the real Glim.
Philosophers still argue which one is you, and if the question has an answer at all.
stickers.tryThis: Put creatures on both branches of the track.

stickers.title: The lever
stickers.riddle: A lever, a cart, and a choice.
lesson: A toy cart rolls to a fork. Creatures sit on both branches.
You can pull the lever or leave it. Either way, someone is in the path.
Many people feel that pulling the lever is worse than leaving it, even when the results match. This puzzle is the trolley problem.
stickers.tryThis: Light the lamp with two creatures behind the wall.

stickers.title: Shadow show
stickers.riddle: What do they see behind the wall?
lesson: One creature sees only the shadows on the screen, and loves them.
Then it meets a real creature that made a shadow. It turns back to the shadows.
Plato told a story of people who see only shadows. We can take a shadow for the world, and even like the shadow more.
stickers.tryThis: Tie four creatures in a line, then poke Kite twice fast.

stickers.title: Telephone
stickers.riddle: Whisper to one, ask the last.
lesson: Kite whispers about a cookie. Each friend passes it on, and it changes a little.
At the end of the chain, the cookie is a monster.
A story that passes through many people changes at each step. When you can, ask the first source.
stickers.tryThis: Make two groups of three, joined by one string. Then snip that string.

stickers.title: The only bridge
stickers.riddle: Snip the one string that holds two.
lesson: Two groups of friends meet through one string.
Cut that string, and news stops crossing between the groups.
Thin links between groups carry new news and new ideas. Sociologists call them weak ties, and they matter more than they look.
stickers.tryThis: Tie four friends to Cap, and tie one more creature only to Cap. Then poke that one.

stickers.title: Your friends have more friends
lesson: Pim has one friend, Cap. Cap has many friends.
A popular creature shows up in many friend lists, so it gets counted again and again.
So most people's friends have more friends than they do. It is math, not a sign that you are unloved. This is the friendship paradox.
stickers.tryThis: You found them all? Start over and try new pairs and new props.
